speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an important and urgent matter.
As the Canadian government is about to export huge quantities of natural gas to the United States, and as this will create the threat of a shortage as well as an increase in the price of natural gas, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin):
That the House reprove the government for that decision which will force Canadians to pay more in the near future for the natural gas produced in their own country.

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS OPPOSING KILLING OF BOWHEAD WHALES- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to put a motion of urgent and pressing importance.
Given that Canada will be sending a delegation to the International Whaling Commission meetings next week, and in view of the fact that the bowhead whale, with a worldwide population of only 1,200, is on the verge of extinction, as verified by the overwhelming weight of international scientific
opinion, and whereas the Canadian government recently published an endangered species list which includes the bowhead whale, upon the recommendation of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan):
That the Canadian delegation to the International Whaling Commission be instructed by this House to oppose absolutely the killing of bowhead whales, and to resist with determination any proposals to allocate quotas for the killing of bowhead whales by the commercial whaling fleets of foreign nations.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REMOVAL OF TAX IN CONNECTION WITH FLIGHT TRAIN ING-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Whereas the federal government recently imposed a 9 per cent sales tax on all new small aircraft and related spare parts purchased by flight training schools which, compounded with a 15 per cent increase in landing fees at most airports as well as landing fee increases at Vancouver, Toronto, Dorval and Mirabel-up from $ 1.65 to $5-has forced these schools to increase their rental rates and lesson charges, and considering how these increases deter the expansion of energy efficient light aircraft travel which is so vital to this country, particularly in remote areas, and that many students take up flying to expand their educational horizons, further facilitating the use of light aircraft travel in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin):
That this government recognize the importance of these flying schools as educational rather than recreational institutions, and remove this tax and roll back increased landing fees which amount to taxation on classrooms in the air which we would not tolerate on conventional classroom facilities.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Two prominent Liberals, former cabinet minister John Turner, and Quebec MNA and former Pepin-Robarts task force member Soulange Chaput-Roland, issued statements over the weekend critical of the approach taken by the Prime Minister to the reform of the constitution.
Madam Chaput-Roland charged that the Prime Minister was needlessly making life difficult for Quebec federalists by his insistence on an early deadline for constitutional reform and his threat to act unilaterally to patriate the constitution, and that the Prime Minister seemed incapable of approaching constitutional questions in other than a confrontationist spirit. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That this House direct the Prime Minister to make a statement before the House recesses as to the government's position on constitutional reform deadlines and the policy of the government respecting the use of referenda for constitutional amendment.

Whereas at least two annual meetings of the U.S.-Canada Parliamentary Committee in Calgary and San Diego have discussed the question of the Alaska pipeline in some detail, and whereas it has been consistently demonstrated at those meetings that an export-directed pre-build pipeline may be in the immediate interests of the United States but, without guarantees, makes as much sense as building the middle floors of a skyscraper without knowing whether or when the upper floors may be built, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):
That this House reaffirms the consistent position of the majority of the Canadian delegation to Canada-U.S. meetings that the Canadian section of the Alaska pipeline will only be built when there are firm and irrevocable guarantees that all sections of this transport pipeline will in fact be built.

subsubtopic: CONDEMNATION OF PERSECUTION OF RELIGIOUS MINORITIES IN IRAN-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a grave matter of urgency which I hope will receive sympathetic support on all sides of this House.
In view of at least 26 more Iranians dying on Monday before a firing squad, including two leaders of the Baha'i religious sect, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille):

FUTURE OF FISHING VESSEL SUBSIDY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, and it concerns the vitally important question of the future of the fishing vessel subsidy program.
This year the minister is operating with an unusually high carryover in his vessel subsidy program due to a number of reasons, the main one being the difficulty the Newfoundland loan board had last year. Because of this high carryover the minister will be unable to approve any new subsidies for this year.
Since the minister indicated that he was attempting to secure additional funding for the program from his colleague, the President of the Treasury Board, so that the program could continue, could he inform the House, today, how successful he has been in securing additional funding for vessel subsidies, so that the fishermen of Atlantic Canada may know what the federal government's intentions are for the subsidy program this year?

speechtext:

This act is about a pipeline as defined in section 2 of the act. Is not the Prime Minister abusing that order in council if he uses it, in effect, to change the whole project?

Madam Speaker, if in fact it was something totally different, then the hon. member would have a very valid point. But everyone who has been talking about the pre-build has not been talking about something totally different: they have been talking about building, in stages, a part of the entire pipeline.
If it were, in some other area, doing some other thing, I think the argument would be that it is a different pipeline. But when you are building a pipeline of a certain distance, and you decide to proceed with one part of it first, you are not doing something different: you are proceeding in stages toward the whole. That is the judgment we have to make-will the whole be built if we do the part. That is a judgment we will be deciding on tomorrow.

Madam Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the Minister of Transport. In view of the fact that Captain Gordon Hallett, of Lockeport, Nova Scotia-master of the Lady Anne III-had to steam 180 miles from Georges Bank to Shelburne, Nova Scotia, due to the inability of the Canadian coastguard to provide a helicopter to save an injured seaman, I ask the Minister of Transport if he is aware of this situation. Madam Speaker, I am not aware of the particular case referred to by the hon. member, but the search and rescue program of my department has been a major preoccupation of mine. I wish to underline the fact that, for example, there will be an increase this year over last year from $3 million to $13 million allocated to the marine aspect of the search and rescue program.
I will inquire about the particular matter referred to, but I want to assure my hon. friend that the search and rescue program is a major preoccupation of both myself and my department.

Since it is obvious our Canadian coastguard, as the minister has indicated, requires improvements in order to cope with our present situation, will the minister consider the construction in Atlantic Canada of at least two additional coastguard ships that are equipped with helicopters in order to more effectively patrol our 200-mile fishing zone? That is a whole lot more water than we ever had to patrol before. We would then be in a position to save the lives of our mariners when catastrophe strikes.

Madam Speaker, a few months ago I rejoiced in the opening of the coastguard college in Sydney, at which time I was present to mark the ceremony. I am now working on the possibility of extending the athletic facilities of that school.

The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-18, an act to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: As hon. members are aware, there are five motions standing on the order paper at the present stage of Bill C-18, an act to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods. All the motions, in the opinion of the Chair, seem to be procedurally acceptable and it is my intention to propose them to the House separately.

Transportation of Dangerous Goods
Motion No. 1
That Bill C-18, an act to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods, be amended in clause 3 by striking out lines 30 to 38 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor:
"this act applies to all vessels of Canadian or foreign registry operating within
the Canadian 200-mile economic zone on the east and west coasts".
He said: Madam Speaker, my brief remarks on this amendment stem from the great concern I have about the weaknesses in this bill. It seems to be drafted in such a way as to present a great many difficulties, not the least of which is that dangerous products transported by sea on the east and west coasts of Canada seem not to be covered by this legislation. In committee we dealt at length with this, and I would like to read into the record of the House what the government proposes in this situation.
In clause 3(5) the government proposes that this legislation not apply to any transporting of dangerous goods in bulk in ships or vessels that is governed by or under the Canada Shipping Act. Subclause (6) says that for the purposes of subclause (5) "in bulk" would mean confined only by the permanent structures of a ship or vessel, without intermediate containment or packaging. As far as we are concerned this eliminates a whole class of transportation in which dangerous goods are being carried, and as a rationale for doing this the government put forward the idea that it is adequately covered in the Canada Shipping Act. I submit that it is not adequately covered in the Canada Shipping Act. I hope we will be able to demonstrate that, but before we do that I point out that Bill C-25 with regard to the same thing-I bring this to the attention of the Conservatives in the House today, and I hope they will be prepared to support my amendments-was silent on this issue. That silence would have allowed the act to pertain to the transporting of dangerous goods on the west coast of Canada and on its east coast under these circumstances. The Conservative bill recognized this problem, and the Conservatives were willing to deal with it, but the Liberal bill presently before us excludes this area of very severe concern.
1 would like to deal with some examples regarding the Canada Shipping Act, which the government feels is adequate to deal with dangerous cargo. If we go back to 1917 and the Mont Blanc in the Halifax harbour, there was a dangerous cargo involved, and its impact was substantial. There are all kinds of examples of this today. We are concerned about preventing loss of life and massive damage which could be caused by commodities carried in large cargoes. The government feels the Canada Shipping Act is adequate. However, a series of sections allow tremendous discretion to the master of a vessel.
The second thing is that if dangerous goods within a vessel are improperly handled, there is a maximum penalty of $1,500. 1 suggest that that is ludicrous and that $1,500 in the present circumstances is just unthinkable. We have argued vehemently that fines of $50,000 and $100,000 are nominal when we look at such things as the Mississauga accident and a variety of other potential accidents. Clearly, the Canada Shipping Act is just a token consideration. It is inadequate. I urge

July 16, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods the government to support this amendment, and I urge the Conservatives also because of a precedent in their bill.
Other members of the government have made a considerable issue of the suggestion that penalties and liabilities imposed are adequate. We have the maritime pollution claims fund, and they claim that as far as oil tankers in our waters are concerned the fund is sufficient. The fund is put up by the Government of Canada through taxing the people who transport dangerous goods, such as oil, up and down the coasts. Hon. members opposite point to a multimillion dollar fund. There are a couple of points 1 would like to make in this regard. That fund is inadequate. We want inspection procedures, and we want penalties which would allow for prevention of accidents. There are not too many people who live on the west coast or on the east coast who are interested in liability or funds to meet liabilities after spills occur.
What we are interested in is prevention, and on that basis I urge the government to support the amendment we have put forward and to allow the transportation of dangerous goods legislation, as weak as it is, to apply to marine transportation and bulk cargoes. There should be a stiffer regime of penalties and more thorough and rigorous inspection procedures.
The government has said that in the liability sphere there is adequate protection for the people of Canada. The government suggests that if there is an accident and a ship blows up or releases a tremendous amount of chlorine gas in some small community on the west coast or the east coast of this country, the liability provisions provided in the Canada Shipping Act are adequate. I will just refer to section 647 in part IV where the maximum liability should an accident occur is 3,100 gold francs for each ton of a ship's tonnage. When we come right down to it, that is S83.50. For a ton of chlorine gas released in a small community-in many communities it is right beside the dock-or for a ton of nitroglycerin or any other dangerous product that amount of $83.50 will not go very far in cleaning up damage or dealing with loss of life or the disruption which would occur.
I suggest that the provision for liability is inadequate. What we are aiming at is prevention, and beyond prevention we are looking at some very weak provisions for liability and for compensating those who will suffer damage. I suggest to the government and to the Conservative members in this House that we require provisions for more stringent penalties for violation and a more rigorous application of inspection procedures.
There is one other feature in this amendment, and that is that the law should apply out to the 200-mile limit. It should go beyond Canada's immediate jurisdiction and its territorial waters. I know that this has been challenged. The United States just recently reiterated that it has no intention of complying with a Canadian law which would impose restrictions on free navigation, as it has been put, or innocent passage of merchant vessels going about their business in the 200-mile limit. The Americans have even extended that statement to suggest that they feel that innocent passage of merchant vessels going about their business, even within territorial
waters, would not respond to Canadian law or any other international law in the area.
I think it is very dangerous to allow such a situation to exist. To quote an example, not too long ago a tug was hauling a barge from Alaska to the lower 48 states. This would have been about May 9, 1980. It was just recently. The barge was carrying a number of barrels containing some very dangerous chemicals. There was a storm and those barrels went overboard. They were clearly beyond our immediate territorial waters, but they were within the 200-mile limit. A barrel washed up onto Canadian territory. What was happening was that an American vessel was carrying extremely dangerous goods in an intermediate container. It was loaded and handled in an improper manner. The end result was that it washed up on a beach in Canada where children could have come along, kicked the barrel open and been killed. The result could have been many other dangerous scenarios.
I would suggest to the government, and again to the many Tory members, especially the ones who come from coastal ridings where this is a possibility, that they have an obligation to vote for this amendment because we have to extend jurisdiction into that economic zone to control the transportation of some of these dangerous goods that are going to affect our citizens.
I would just like to elaborate a little more on this particular example because the Americans, when they were aware that those dangerous goods were floating free in the ocean and in danger of washing up in Canada and creating a danger to Canadian citizens, did not bother notifying Canada or assisting in the search for those goods. We became involved in a token search and, if you reflect back a little further, we sent a bill to the Russians for doing exactly the same thing and insisted on payment for a very costly search. I think in this particular incident we should have conducted a thorough search, and should have submitted a bill for that search to the United States, with a very stern reprimand for acting in a very negligent manner on this issue. There is a vacuum in the law here, Mr. Speaker. We should have a law that allows us to exert jurisdiction in this matter over the 200-mile limit. We have set a precedent for it.
We have the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) here.

Perhaps the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) might be concerned about this issue because it does relate to our relations with the United States. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, the problem in front of us is what we have to do to apply Canadian jurisdiction in this area. My amendment, I am certain, if accepted by the government and some of the Tories in the same area, would fill this vacuum. In the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act we have simply said that vessels that are going to be working within Arctic waters, even though they are not technically within our territorial waters, are going to submit a declaration that goods are
July 16, 1980

carried in a manner which conforms to the regulations. They are going to submit, if necessary, to an inspection before those vessels travel in those waters. 1 suggest to the government that the same thing should occur here.
Many vessels have been built to carry particular products. Once cleared and the passage worked out, there would be no problem. What we are looking at is the rather ad hoc itinerant traffic which carries dangerous drums of chemicals in an improper manner and proceeds to a 200-mile limit where we might want to have a declaration stating how those goods are to be carried and how to protect Canadian citizens from being harmed by these dangerous goods. We might want to inspect those vessels, or least have the opportunity to do so. 1 would submit to the government that this amendment provides that mechanism.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I think that the Conservatives, by leaving their bill silent on this issue left the opportunity open under section 28 for the minister to make regulations dealing with this. It provided an opportunity, should we need it, to fill this vacuum. The Liberal bill clearly does not provide an opportunity to move into this area if it is demonstrated to be necessary. Their plea that the Canada Shipping Act and maritime conventions fill the bill is clearly inadequate, and I would ask them to withdraw that. I submit that $1,500 in this day and age is a completely inadequate penalty. The liability provisions are inadequate when we look at some of the things that are going on around the world, the enormous costs of clean-up and repair of damages. So what we need is a stronger regime of penalties and a more rigorous inspection.
In the final analysis, what we have off the west coast of Canada is the example of the American tug dropping barrels into the sea. We have the example of tankers of chlorine lying at the bottom of Malaspina channel which could rise and create a cloud of chlorine gas around certain areas. There are numerous members of the House in both parties who have said they are opposed to tanker traffic and the tremendous danger it could create going up and down the coast. What I would ask them today is to stand up and be counted in supporting this amendment and at least to keep faith with many of the election promises they have made.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we submit that the transportation of dangerous goods involved in ships should remain subject to the Canada Shipping Act regulations. The regulation of bulk cargoes which fall within the specific or general connotation of dangerous goods involves matters of ship design, construction and operation. In the case of crude oil and refined petroleum, tankers are specially designed, taking into account the dangerous nature of cargoes carried as it affects the requirements for hull, machinery, and additional safety equipment.
The Intergovernmental Maritime Consultative Organization establishes the code for the construction of equipment of ships carrying liquefied gases in bulk. The same organization has established a code for the construction and equipment of ships carrying dangerous bulk chemicals. In other words, the ship
Transportation of Dangerous Goods itself is the container. In the case of bulk cargoes, by far the majority are carried in vessels for which the hulls are of a particular design to load, transport and discharge such cargoes under safe conditions, including special consideration of matters such as stability, ventilation, and measures against inroads of the sea. All of the above require the full range of disciplines, that is, naval architecture, marine engineering and nautical sciences which are required to make and implement regulations which come under the Canada Shipping Act dealing with the safe design, construction and operation of any ship.
In all of the above cases, vessels are required to carry certificates of inspection, certificates of fitness, and international convention certificates which are issued under the Canada Shipping Act. Any vessels in Canadian territorial waters are already subject to Canadian legislation. Canadian vessels anywhere in the world are subject to Canadian legislation, and that is under the Canada Shipping Act in the case of bulk shipping.
The second effect that this amendment would have is that it would be a motion which would be in discord with the Territorial Seas and Fishing Zones Act which establishes the limits of Canadian jurisdiction over the seas to something like 12 miles. This would also be declared ultra vires by a court as trying to impose Canadian jurisdiction over waters which are not within the scope of this bill. Therefore it is the view of the government that this motion should be opposed.

Mr. Speaker, what the hon. member from the NDP has indicated is that there are certain limitations to this bill which possibly can be governed by section 28 of the act and also by the regulations. But I think that is one of the major weaknesses of the bill in that, to a large extent, we are looking to the regulations to handle the requirements of the act. This is an umbrella bill. It does not attend to the problems in itself, which are presented by the movement of dangerous goods.
I raise this point because many residents in my riding of Etobicoke Centre have become very concerned about the movement of dangerous goods in the past year, particularly following the disaster in Mississauga. May I remind hon. members that the disaster occurred five to seven minutes west of the borough of Etobicoke where there are many residents who would have been affected by an accident of that kind. Of even greater concern is that last year again there was considerable discussion of the plans of CP Rail to add a third rail line in Etobicoke, which in itself would allow for increased freight movement and increased speed of such freight movement. Some of the houses directly affected by this third rail are only 50 feet from the proposed line.
In January there was a hearing of the Canadian Transport Commission on this whole matter. In the opinion of the residents most affected, it was a very unsatisfactory hearing. They applied to the department, as well as the Department of Justice, for counsel to be supported by the public purse in order to present their case, which is a very broad case affecting

July 16, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
many, many parts of the country, in particular many parts of the city of Toronto. This was turned down, and at very short notice the residents were required to present their own case to the CTC. They felt the results were not satisfactory, and they are anxiously awaiting the results of that hearing before any further action will be taken.
1 wish to address the question of regulations this afternoon because, unfortunately, as has been the case in many pieces of legislation brought forward by the government opposite, much government in this country is by regulation now. Those regulations, as they apply to this act, will make or break the intent of the act. On a number of occasions I have urged the minister to consult widely on the form and the content of these regulations. I have urged him to educate himself on the practice of shippers and the concerns of residents most directly affected.
In particular I asked the minister if he would be interested in meeting with representatives of the Metropolitan Toronto Rail Action Committee. I think the committee now is composed of over 15 ratepayers' associations in the metropolitan Toronto area that have vital concerns about the movement of rail transport through residential areas of metro Toronto. To date the minister has not seen fit to meet with these representatives.
Today I want to put on record concerns expressed to me at ratepayers' association meetings. Freight moving from Sarnia to points east and north of metropolitan Toronto moves right through residential areas of metropolitan Toronto such as Etobicoke, Parkdale, Rosedale, Don Valley West, East York, and into parts of Scarborough.
Recently 1 mentioned in the House that CP Rail is soliciting business out of Michigan to move goods to the New England States through residential parts of metropolitan Toronto. There is movement back and forth in the delivery of dangerous goods in the Toronto area, over to Scarborough and back to points west of Scarborough. They do not feel this increased movement of dangerous goods is necessary. Finally, dangerous chemicals are shipped from Sarnia, through metroplitan Toronto to Montreal, and similar types of chemicals are shipped from Montreal to Toronto and points west of Toronto. The people in M-TRAC feel it is worth considering whether there can be some exchange of these chemicals. As I understand it, basically they are similar chemicals with different trade or product names.
These are some of the concerns which have been expressed. 1 believe they must be dealt with in the regulations. 1 appreciate some of these things must be dealt with by regulation, and 1 am sorry others are not dealt with directly in the act. As I have said, on four occasions I have implored the minister to meet with representatives of M-TRAC before these regulations are brought down. I have done this through personal conversation, by letter, by a motion under Standing Order 43, and also recently with a question in the House. By consulting personally, by hearing first hand the concerns, and by attending a meeting of the affected residents, I am sure the minister will have a much better understanding of the direction which the
people directly affected in residential areas feel the regulations should take.
My final point concerns the whole area of inspection and the administration of the regulations under the act. The inspector plays a very delicate role, and the minister must give a very delicate set of directions to the inspector. On the one hand, he must be aware of and concerned for the interests of the shippers so that the economic costs of the administration of the act do not outweigh the benefits achieved. On the other hand, he must not be totally concerned with the concerns of the shippers because it is the people living in the areas that are so close who are directly affected. My riding of Etobicoke Centre is affected in two ways. It is affected by the CP Rail line going through the centre of Etobicoke and also the major highway running through the centre of Etobicoke. 1 ask the minister to take great care in the direction he gives to the inspectors in order that the administration of the act will not favour unduly the interests of one side or the other affected by the regulations concerned.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to intervene very briefly just to place another view of the amendment in front of us. The remarks of the parliamentary secretary are shared largely by the official opposition, but I want to extend the parameters touched upon by the mover of the amendment. This brings the whole question of marine transport somewhat into focus.
I think it is fair to say that in the course of discussing this matter in committee there was an interjection by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Penner) which I thought had a lot of validity. It caused some extensive discussion with respect to the attitude of this House to sea-marine matters in general. I think the proper or the best way to dispose of the concerns raised by members of the New Democratic Party in this respect will be realized when the chamber gets on with the work of dealing with books 3, 4, and 5 of the Maritime Code. We have books 1 and 2, with the exception of the coastal shipping provisions.
The hope of all of us in this chamber-certainly those members on this side-is that when the House resumes in the fall or at an early date into the new session the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) will move himself, if that is at all possible, to put before the chamber the provisions contained in books 3, 4 and 5 of the new Maritime Code. Having said that and reiterated that, it is only when we have had a discussion in this chamber and in committee with the industry and community of interests involved that we will begin to address ourselves to the major and significant outstanding problem in marine transportation in this country.
With that caveat, and with the understanding given to us by the parliamentary secretary and others during the course of the discussion of the amendment in committee, I would indicate to the parliamentary secretary that we are prepared to support the position of the government so that we might not mislead anybody into believing that Bill C-18 contained provi-
July 16, 1980

sions that, in our view, are sufficient to meet all of the concerns which are very broad and obviously go beyond the requirements of the bill,

Mr. Speaker, 1 just want to make a last ditch appeal to the parliamentary secretary. I wish the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Guigan) would not leave just yet since this is something he will end up having to deal with. The monkey will be on his back. I see he has left anyway.
The limit of Canadian jurisdiction-12 miles or 200 miles- under our economic and fisheries zones, begs the question. The reasons given by the parliamentary secretary for the government not wishing to accept this amendment border on unreasoning stubbornness. If, as, and when the Canada Shipping Act is amended, it will provide more adequate law covering the transportation of dangerous goods in bulk in vessels up to 200 miles out to sea. That would be fine, but we are not going to get such a provision tomorrow.
At the moment the situation is that a rust bucket flying a Panamanian or Roumanian flag and carrying a SI million cargo on which it can collect up to $300,000 in freight charges, say, might be liable to a fine of $1,500 under the Canada Shipping Act. That is surely sufficient evidence of the lack of provisions under that act.
I am not optimistic that there will be any speedy amendments to the Canada Shipping Act which would bring its provisions and its jurisdiction up to the standards of the transportation of dangerous goods act. We might get some amendments every year or two or three years.
1 would say to my good friend, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), that I am even less optimistic about any kind of speedy decisions on all aspects of the Maritime Code. They will take another two or three years.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, as and when the government amends the Canada Shipping Act and as and when the Maritime Code is revised, they could then include in appropriate legislation the repeal of this provision that we are proposing in the transportation of dangerous goods act.
My point is that the Canada Shipping Act is inadequate. The Maritime Code is not in place. Until such time as those two measures are in place and are sufficient, surely we need some kind of measure that covers these dangerous bulk commodities in vessels up to 200 miles out to sea, in our economic and fisheries zones.
When the government brings in amendments to the Canada Shipping Act it could repeal this particular amendment, if it were accepted today. That may be a year or two years from now. This party fails to understand the government's unwillingness to make a provision to see us through this interim period at least. I would hope that the officials in the House who are here to provide assistance to the House and to the parliamentary secretary would quickly send a note to him saying, "With those kinds of things that we have here in the future about the Canada Shipping Act and the Maritime
Transportation of Dangerous Goods Code, this amendment could be accepted until such time as we do the other pieces of legislation."
This is just too big a problem, with the possibility of a disaster, because of the transportation of a dangerous commodity in bulk in some rust bucket 100 miles off our coast on which we can impose only a $1,500 fine. It is not as if we have not had problems in other instances, whether with the British government, the Russian government or whatever. We do not have anything in place that is of any consequence and that would serve as an incentive for maritime shippers to do a better job with the transportation of dangerous goods in bulk or that would deter them from taking any chances. All it is going to cost them is a $1,500 fine out of a freight charge of $100,000 or more. They will take their chances and pay the $1,500 fine.
That is all we are asking for, Mr. Speaker. We are not suggesting this would be the be all and end all forever. Until the Canada Shipping Act and the Maritime Code are amended, however, we do not have anything to cover this kind of situation. 1 hope the parliamentary secretary will reconsider the government's position on the amendment and will accept it.

Motion No. 2
That Bill C-18, an act to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods, be amended by deleting clause 10 at page 6 and substituting the following therefor:
"10. It is sufficient proof of the offence to establish that it was committed by
an employee or agent of the accused whether or not the employee or agent is
identified or has been prosecuted for the offence."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment endeavours to do away with what has happened too many times in various areas of the transportation industry in Canada. Where there is wind and where there has been a mishap, a spill or an accident, too often the employee on the ground or the employee next to it, is taken out of service, is given demerit marks, is subpoenaed to a coroner's inquest or is charged with manslaughter or a lesser offence. This amendment would make companies responsible for the actions of their employees. The way the bill reads at the moment it could encourage a sort of fancy footwork on the part of corporate lawyers and officers, trying to fit corporate activities into definitions of reasonable.
In particular, clause 10 invites corporations to avoid penalty by pointing fingers at specific employees. We contend that the only way to ensure compliance with the act and its regulations in the corporate context is to impress upon corporate directors, officers and officials the fact that the corporation will be liable for the actions of its employees. If that is law, then surely one can be more reasonably confident that the corporation will be sure to give proper instructions and see to the carrying out of those instructions by its employees. 1 do not suggest that if an employee was wilfully negligent, the corporation would not be absolved. I submit that if through a court, hearing or inquiry, the corporation can prove that it carried out proper instructions, continuing instructions, supervision, and seeing to it that the employees followed those instructions and implemented them, then it is not to blame. However, if an employee still wilfully, criminally and deliberately disobeyed those instructions, then that employee would still be liable in those kinds of circumstances.
I would like to cite an example from my own experience during my many years on the railroad. It involves a section foreman who was awarded the prize by the company for three years in a row for maintaining the best section in the whole division. When there was a mishap and eight cars were in the ditch and a locomotive was upside down, it was felt that a broken rail was the cause. Who received the demerit marks, was taken out of service and lost pay? It was that section foreman. He had carried out all the procedures available to him which he had been instructed to follow by the company. But though the company had reduced its maintenance procedures, lengthened the number of miles of track that he was to patrol and reduced his crew from four men to three men to two men, he still had to inspect the track adequately. Of course, he was just not able to do the job even though he worked after hours and did not put in any claims for overtime. This section foreman was the one who received demerit marks and was taken out of service.
None of the company officers or the corporation itself was given a slap on the wrist for what was obviously inadequate maintenance, provision of personnel, equipment and worn out rails. The employee was the one who got it. Surely our amendment covers that kind of situation. If an employee wilfully, deliberately and negligently disobeys the instructions, training and use of the equipment and material provided to him to provide for the safe transportation of dangerous goods, he is still individually liable. We are trying to plug the availability to officers, and corporate lawyers on behalf of corporations of the move which leaves the blame placed upon the shoulders of one or more individual employees.
It is a collective responsibility, and the first part of the responsibility belongs to the corporation concerned. We hope that the government has reconsidered its position since we discussed this matter in committee and that it is now prepared to accept this amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that this bill is not only designed for the railroads.
I was using the railroads as an example.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) used the example of the railroads. This bill applies to all modes of transportation, all people who contract or are engaged in that work. The deletion set out in motion No. 2 is a very serious one since it removes any possible defence on the part of any employer for the employees' actions and would make the employer liable even if he could show that he exercised reasonable care. In other words, he is presumed to be guilty without proof or identification. In other words, it changes the common law doctrine which absolves an employer for liability for the actions of its employees outside the course of their normal duties.
This amendment would conceivably encourage carelessness, negligence, recklessness and subvert the legislative or regulatory controls normally applicable to employees. The government recommends that this motion be opposed.

Motion No. 3
That Bill C-18, an act to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods, be amended in clause 17 by striking out line 23 at page 13 and substituting the following therefor:
"sion or escape and shall, as soon as possible in the circumstances, restore the
natural environment as nearly as practicable to its previous condition."
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion we are proposing here would require those in charge of dangerous goods which were involved in an accident during their transportation to restore the natural environment, as nearly as practicable, to its previous condition following that accident. I appreciate that the government is up tight because it does not want matters of the environment in this bill to the extent where it transgresses other environmental laws, either federal, provincial or municipal. We appreciate that fact.
We believe, from what legal advice we were able to obtain without fee, that anywhere and everywhere we used the word "environment" in this legislation or in our amendment, it applies only as it relates to or is as the result of the transportation of dangerous goods, and nothing else. This motion applies to the environment only with regard to incidental transportation, so as not to invade what might otherwise be of provincial jurisdiction or municipal jurisdiction.
There could be room for the constitutional argument that provincial environment legislation does not apply to railway accidents. We submit that there is room because that is an area of federal jurisdiction. This amendment would fill such a gap. There could be an equivalent justifiable argument with regard to interprovincial trucking. Each province may rule upon rates, conditions of transport and so on, and even agree upon these subjects interprovincially. In other words, the federal government has allowed the provinces to have most of the say in matters of interprovincial trucking.
We submit that in the transportation of dangerous goods interprovincially and where one province's laws and regulations are lax and weak compared to its neighbouring province and there is a spill which harms the environment, this law would apply. It would apply with regard to the process of cleaning up and fixing up the local environment after the spill, in other words, restoring it to its original state as much as is practicable. That is all we are asking. This restoration would come after, and sometimes long after, the emergency measures to remedy dangerous conditions have been completed. Therefore, it would not interfere with any immediate or current emergency measures. It has been suggested in committee that this amendment would interfere with any kind of emergency action being taken immediately upon an accident. We submit that that is not the case. I want also to remind the House that our point of view of this coincides with what has been recommended by the Canadian Environmental Law Association.
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
I am not a lawyer, and I confess that we have relied to a great degree on the opinion of those eminent legal people who have specialized in law as it relates to the environment. Their work in fact recognizes that any amendments to this legislation in terms of the environment must be restricted only to where it pertains to the transportation of dangerous goods and nothing beyond that. Federal or provincial environment laws would take place, take effect, or take over anything beyond that harms the environment as it relates to the transportation of dangerous goods.
We think the government worries overly much on this one, that the amendment is restrictive enough, that it would not interfere with provincial autonomy or jurisdiction. In fact it could fill some gaps probably welcomed by many provinces. I understand the provinces have been most co-operative in discussions with the government on joint action in implementing this legislation. We feel that the amendment is narrow enough to apply only to the environment being restored as a result of a spill or an accident due to the transportation of dangerous goods, and nothing beyond that.
We hope that the government has reconsidered and thought about the arguments that we have put forward, and has had a recommendation from the officials that this amendment will be acceptable.

Mr. Speaker, the clause in its original form was meant to handle emergency measures consistent with basic public safety. This would hold any person having the responsibility to report or having "the charge, management or control of goods" to restore the natural environment after an accident even if that person is in no way responsible for the emission or discharge. This motion interferes with the provinces' control. It would conflict with environmental protection legislation being enacted in the provinces. I repeat, a person having the charge, management or control of dangerous goods may not have caused or even contributed to the causation of the discharge and thus should not be held responsible for this activity.
The actions needed for restoration of the environment might be completely beyond the resources of the person burdened by this proposed responsibility. We recommend that this motion be opposed.

Motion No. 4
That Bill C-18, an act to promote public safety in the transportation of dangerous goods, be amended in clause 20 by striking out lines 6 to 8 at page 16 and substituting the following therefor:
"danger to the health or safety of the public or damage or danger to property
or the environment, the minister may direct a public inquiry to be made in the
manner directed".
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a long struggle. 1 want to say at the outset, and I wanted to say it earlier, that members from all parties in the House and in the committee along with officials in the department have done a lot of work on this bill so I do not want in any way to denigrate the great efforts made by members of the committee, the parliamentary secretary and the officials. But again we have an amendment that we feel improves and strengthens the legislation. All parties are agreed that we want the legislation. I do not think there is any disagreement that wherever we can improve or strengthen it, all parties should do so.
Our motion No. 4, would add danger or damage to the environment to the list of reasons for calling an inquiry into the spill of dangerous goods during transportation. It would also provide for public hearings. Again, we have been very careful to word our amendment to make it as narrow as possible so that there is no way that it could go beyond this legislation. There is no way it could interfere with, contravene or in any other way injure the interests of a province which has jurisdiction, or in any way encroach upon federal or provincial environmental laws that apply to everything else other than the transportation of dangerous goods. We have tried to be exceedingly careful in the wording or our amendment.
I think there was general consensus and agreement by all sides in the House concerning the validity and desirability of providing for public hearings. I am confident that there is no argument on that aspect of our amendment.
The Canadian Railway Labour Association in its submissions to the committee and to the government has called for public hearings. The committee accepted an amendment of ours which we appreciated. It requires the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to publish all inquiry reports instead of being able to keep them confidential. We appreciate the amendment
that was accepted in the committee was useful, and wc appreciate it being accepted by the government and all other members of the committee. But this motion No. 4 would extend public participation and information a little bit further, including environment as the result-and I repeat

of an accident or a spill as a result of the transportation of dangerous goods. Therefore, it would include environment only in that narrow context as a reason to hold an inquiry as recommended not only by the Canadian Railway Labour Association but the Canadian Environmental Law Associaton.
I believe our motion says "The minister may". It does not say "He shall". It says "The minister may direct a public inquiry." He may direct an inquiry into other aspects than arc in the bill. We are only adding the aspect of environment where the minister may direct an inquiry. That may be immediately upon, close to, subsequent to, or some time after a mishap in the transportation of dangerous goods as it affects the environment.
The example cited by my colleague the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skeliy) of tank cars of chlorine gas lying at the bottom of an inlet may not produce effects on the environment that can be seen until several years after the mishap. That occurred during the transportation of dangerous goods. If those tank cars rust, as they will, the chlorine gas will escape. Some community may be affected and therefore evacuated. Surely it is not beyond good reason and good sense to have a law whereby the minister may cause a public inquiry to be held as a result of the aftermath of that mishap and the subsequent leakage as it affects the environment. Even if it does not affect any people, it will certainly affect the environment. The minister and his officials may use their own good judgment, and I am assuming the word "good", in all cases. Surely it is not unreasonable to have that in the law.
As the bill reads now, if Mississauga or MacGregor had happened in some isolated area where there was no immediate danger to life or property, the minister could not call an inquiry. Had those mishaps occurred in an isolated area and the only damage was to the environment, and not to persons or property, nothing else would have happened. The stuff would just lie around. Who would inquire into or have the responsibility when it only affects the environment?
This amendment is deliberately narrow enough for the government to accept easily that it be incorporated into the law. I am perfectly prepared to trust and rely upon this and subsequent ministers of transport to use their good sense and judgment as to whether to call a public inquiry as it affects the danger to life, property or the environment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to make a few comments at this stage. I shall be brief, but I hope the parliamentary secretary will pay attention to what I have to say.
I know there have been four attempts in recent years to pass legislation of this nature. It is extremely important, therefore, that we should get the bill through as quickly as possible because we all have an interest in improving the situation with regard to the transportation of dangerous goods. This desire is highlighted by the Mississauga train derailment last year. One result of that accident was an increased public awareness of the need to establish rules governing the transportation of dangerous goods.
The House should remember that while accidents on the scale of Mississauga do not happen every day, thank goodness, other accidents with very serious ramifications do occur frequently. I saw one such accident just the other night while driving from Ottawa to Kingston-and I might say that that in itself is a hazardous occupation! Just the other night, though, I was confronted at first hand with the result of a

July 16, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods
transport truck accident involving the spillage of powdered caustic soda, a very corrosive substance. The driver of the truck was badly burned by the soda, and members of the emergency crew who was there to help out were also burned. This came about because the truck driver and the others closely involved were not immediately washed down-it was not known for some time whether or not water would aggravate the situation.
While we can make provision for special handling, packaging and labelling of dangerous goods, we must also see to it that the various emergency services receive adequate training to enable them to deal with the results of accidents involving such cargoes. I have in mind members of police, fire and ambulance services.
In the past several months a great deal of concern has been expressed throughout eastern Ontario with regard to shipments of radioactive nuclear waste. The parliamentary secretary will be aware of this. Much of the public awareness has come about as a result of publication of an excellent series of articles on this subject in The Kingston Whig-Standard highlighting the dangers which are inherent in shipping radioactive nuclear waste. In this case spent reactor fuel which has become highly radioactive after use at Chalk River is shipped some 1,100 miles to a United States refining centre in South Carolina. The route of these shipments passes through much of eastern Ontario, a section of the country which is fairly thickly populated.
I know it was explained to us in committee that when this material is shipped, a security plan is in effect and that the police are made aware of its movement. But who else is made aware of its movement? Are other emergency services, such as ambulance crews, made aware of it? It would appear that apart from the police none of the emergency personnel such as fire and ambulance people are told. And even if they were to be informed, do they have adequate training and knowledge to enable them to deal at a moment's notice with the kind of accident which might take place? It would appear not.
I would draw the attention of the parliamentary secretary to the statement made in committee by Mr. Beare of the Atomic Energy Control Board. According to him, the only training offered to emergency officials who might be called upon to deal with a nuclear accident is a one-week once-a-year course at Chalk River. Mr. Beare suggested that the AECB and the Department of Transport might work together to provide special courses for fire and other emergency officials who could be called upon to deal with accidents. I might add that at the present time similar joint courses between the two agencies are being held to train mine inspectors. This is an example of the way in which we might go about making training available to officials who might have to deal with a nuclear accident.
I believe it is incumbent upon the minister to proceed along the lines of this suggestion and apply it across the board to those who might have to deal with an accident resulting from the transportation of dangerous goods. Far too few of them receive adequate training at present to enable them to do so, as
was certainly exemplified in the case of the accident I witnessed the other night.
There is one other matter I should like to draw to the attention of the parliamentary secretary. A study done recently by a consumer group in the United States has shown that the shipper who has the contract to take the nuclear waste from Chalk River to the United States plant in South Carolina had 152 accidents while moving nuclear material in the period between 1974 and 1978. The shippers of that company had these accidents during that period. Yet officials in AECL who give out the contracts claim that the company's past record is very good. So on one hand we have particulars as to the accident rate of that company or its shippers in the United States while on the other, here in Canada, AECL is saying they have an excellent record. I am worried that the agencies responsible for regulating the shipment of nuclear material are not as impartial as they might be.
I would like to ask if a study similar to the one done in the United States has been carried out by AECL. We do not know. We simply have to accept on faith that the shipper is a responsible company and that AECL is regulating it just as closely as it should be. I just do not want to go on the word of AECL without seeing documentation to back up that claim.
I think the parliamentary secretary would agree that a company's accident record should be a major consideration when it comes to contracting the movement of nuclear materials.
I said that I do not wish to delay these proceedings any longer than they have to be, but I express the very sincere hope that the parliamentary secretary-and through him the minister-will agree that these points are certainly worth considering, that they are very important, and that he will see that they are put into effect just as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I want to preface my remarks at third reading by saying again that all members of the committee, departmental officials, the parliamentary secretary and the minister did much work on this legislation. I particularly want to recognize the assistance officials gave us with their comments and their answers. We did not necessarily like them all, but the officials were very forthcoming during the committee hearings, and I wish that
Transportation of Dangerous Goods could happen on every piece of legislation with which we deal in this place.
While all parties support the passage of legislation regarding the transportation of dangerous goods, as legislators we also have an obligation to tell the public that this act will not eliminate all of our concerns about the movement of hazardous substances.
The illusion that this act will prevent disasters must be dispelled. Some day another train, truck, ship or plane will spill its deadly cargo on an unsuspecting neighbourhood, shattering what is presently being looked upon as the security- and we call it false security-of this legislation. Maybe luck will be with us again and the neighbourhood can be evacuated. Let us hope so.
What the act will do is provide for proper classification, packaging and identification of all dangerous goods being transported-with stiff penalties for non-compliance-which in itself is significant, but it will not deal with safety of transport vehicles per se. In fact, the following statement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Transport, indicates that. He said:
It is important to note that the bill does not establish safety standards and procedures respecting the safe operation of any mode of transport or any industrial activity ... it addresses only the special question of dangerous goods.
In other words, this legislation will not, for example, require adequate maintenance of railway lines or trucks or prevent some worn out boxcar somewhere on a train from causing the derailment of another car carrying chlorine, for example. The government is leaving policing of safety to other authorities such as the Canadian Transport Commission, but the CTC must be given the resources to do the job.
In the past three years the staff of the Canadian Transport Commission, including staff in the rail safety division, has been cut back. There is no argument that that kind of restraint must be lifted, yesterday. In fact the estimates have called for a progressive reduction in the number of safety inspectors working for the CTC over the last three years under three different governments, two Liberal and one Tory.
There are some shortcomings with regard to our dangerous goods legislation which need government attention. For example, there is no opportunity for the general public to make representations regarding the adequacy of the legislation's regulations, although government members did support an amendment of ours to provide freedom of information regarding reports of inquiries into accidents involving dangerous goods.
The legislation should also be amended further to include a compensation scheme, funded by industry and administrated by the government, which could compensate people for immediate needs after a disaster and then collect expenses from those responsible for a spill later on through the courts. This would avoid such situations as the one at Mississauga, for example, where the CPR provided money only for immediate needs, if people signed away their rights to further action. Let us remember that we are looking at possible damages of

July 16, 1980
Transportation of Dangerous Goods hundreds of millions of dollars in some cases. What if the company concerned went bankrupt? Who pays?
I suppose the best way to reduce damages is to improve safety. In conjunction with this legislation the railways must be required to modernize their operations and hire adequate complements of staff to inspect and maintain facilities. We can have all the transportation of dangerous goods legislation we like, but if the facilities and infrastructure for the transportation of dangerous goods are worn out or inadequate, this legislation will be of little help. It will be after the fact.
Would you believe, Mr. Speaker, that between 1956 and 1977 the railways alone eliminated 60,000 jobs, 30,000 of which were cut from maintenance, directly affecting safety, not just in the transportation of dangerous goods but all other kinds of safety? Of course the railways should not be singled out. I only use that as an example. More stringent safety procedures must be required of all modes of transportation, and I draw that to the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) because 1 presume that a satellite carrying radioactive material is transporting a dangerous good, and international, let alone the national, ramifications must be apparent to him as well.
If public concern over Mississauga or MacGregor is translated into shifting the movement of dangerous goods from rail to truck, we will not be better off; in fact, we could be worse off. However, the reality is that the Minister of Transport is not God, and he has professed that on a number of occasions. Even with the most stringent regulations, even with a bill with many teeth in it, even if the transport companies did everything humanly possible to prevent accidents, some accidents will occasionally occur. This legislation will not solve all of that, but this does not mean that we cannot significantly reduce the number of accidents, which must, in the short run, be the primary objective. However, some will be missing the boat if we do not emphasize the long-term solution to be the reduction of our society's dependence on non-renewable materials which are themselves dangerous or are made from dangerous goods.
Chemical technology is outstripping our knowledge of its effects. Sixty-three thousand man-made chemicals are now in use, a thousand more are added to the list each year. Transportation is only one aspect of the problem. There is also the manufacture, storage and disposal of these projects. As a society we should ask ourselves if we want to continue producing so many hazardous goods and if we should not be treating them comprehensively from the cradle to the grave.
My purpose in making these remarks is not to alarm unduly but rather to point out that the job has just begun and we should not be content to rest on this one piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I also will be very brief with respect to this piece of legislation. As we know, the need for this type of bill, for bringing together a number of perceived areas, started back
seven or eight years ago under that distinguished gentleman who is now in the other place, the then minister of transport, Senator Jean Marchand. At the time the only real concerns which were being contemplated were in the areas of road transportation, as has been mentioned. But over the years there has been an evolution of thought, a continuation of very dedicated work by officials, indeed, a succession of bills, starting with Bill C-53, followed by C-70, C-25, and now C-18 in front of us. Because each one of them has changed and grown, they have demonstrated the need for a comprehensive piece of legislation, one which at once affords levels of protection which a bill like this can accomplish but at the same time provides us with a legislative basis upon which regulations can be brought forward which will lend substance to the protection of the public and, as my friend the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) keeps referring to it, the environment, because that is not unimportant in this context.
1 recognize, together with those requirements, requirements for the safe handling, identification, training, proper inspection, a little light on investigation, a little light on where transport begins or ends. On the other hand, it seems to me that the perceived requirements of society here in Canada today-and I think this is rather important-should not place undue economic or legal restraint upon the private sector, or where applicable the public sector, which must, on a daily and continuing basis, move dangerous or hanzardous projects around the country. That in itself is no small achievement, brought about by the collective efforts of a small but dedicated branch within transport which is responsible for dangerous goods and a succession of ministers of transport.
The bill as well presents us with some pretty broad guidelines which are fully understood by the provinces, guidelines with respect to regulations which will flow from them. These are pretty broad and clearly understandable guidelines, not only to provincial authorities but to industry and the community of interest which will have to operate within them.
The bill is comprehensive and it lends the necessary statutory authority which at this time is perceivable to all of us. It may not, as some of us might have wished, have gone a little further in certain areas, but I do not believe that to be a limitation on the capacity of this bill because if bills of this nature, indeed most legislation which comes before the House in this broad category, are not living, breathing things capable of change from time to time which reflect need, change in regulation which accommodates that need, change in the legislative character by way of amendment here on the floor of the House to accommodate need, if we have not achieved at least that in this bill, then I believe it could be properly said that we have failed. On the contrary, this bill means all of this.
If the distinguished member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski) were here, he might want to make that point today and to emphasize that there is not a single thing in this piece of legislation that puts any barrier in front of the regulatory process to accommodate, and that is what we have set out to do. I think that if the former minister of transport were here he might have made another point with some pride, that is,
July 16, 1980

that as we have developed over the years-1 suppose other former ministers of transport could also take some pride in this-as this bill and its regulations have developed and are yet to be clearly and finally set forth, we have been leaders and not followers.
The bill is innovative in its approach to the statutory requirement for regulation and it has been paralleled by neighbours to the south. In short, we have been the leaders not the followers in the development of comprehensive and, in my judgment, good legislation. The bill was produced with the fullest and broadest co-operation of the industry, the provinces, our neighbours to the south, and indeed a very broad range within the international community that will be subject to this law when in fact they are in operation in whatever mode in this country. It was acceptable to them; it was clear and concise, in their judgment. Again I think that is a credit to the process which brought this together.
As I have indicated, all of us should show some respect and appreciation for that small but very active group within the department who have responsibilities in this area. We have some obligation to wish them well and thank them for the nitty-gritty of putting together the regulations under it. I am satisfied on two accounts. I am satisfied with the competency of that staff and the innate good sense of the chamber to react to need when it is perceived, although seven years might be described as a damnable length of time to achieve and accomplish something as fundamentally good and sound.
Generally we on this side of the House are satisfied that the bill provides capacity for easy amendment and flexible regulations in areas where it falls short, where it fails, or where new understanding is required of intermodal movement of goods in this country, in and out of it, through and over it, or around its waters. I have less certainty respecting the administration of this bill and would express the hope that the wherewithal, as mentioned by other members in their deliberations, for adequate training will be made available. Certainly the Canadian Transport Commission is one vehicle, but it is not the only one. The inspection services contemplated as being the inspection authority within the meaning of this act, no matter what other act they may be operative under, require assistance in the form of upgrading their information, professionalism, and capacity to ensure that this bill and its regulations operate in the interest of Canadians, that it operates effectively in the protection of our environment without infringing upon the jurisdiction of the provinces.
In the course of its public hearings respecting this bill, the committee heard a wide cross-section of Canadians, including consumer groups. I think this morning we were criticized by one consumer group that we had failed as a committee or as a Parliament to pay attention to its views. Simply that is not so. In putting together the list of witnesses, the Standing Committee on Transport was conscious of the broad section of briefs which came before it. The committee chose representative groups and acted arbitrarily. I will explain why in a moment,
Transportation of Dangerous Goods but it accommodated the broadest interests of groups. In response to dozens of briefs, the government-and it is a credit to them-offered numerous amendments. We heard the concern of the New Democratic Party for amendments in certain areas. We on this side offered and debated amendments to this piece of legislation. So I think it has had good public exposure before arriving here this afternoon.
As I indicated, the bill is a living thing, and as with all such living things it will grow and change from time to time. I am confident that in that growth and change, because of its character and nature, it will reflect the legitimate needs of the safety of people and the environment. I am satisfied it is in competent hands. That leaves only to be said that we on this side extend our appreciation to the parliamentary secretary for the knowledgeable and professional manner in which he dealt with this matter in committee and in the House. We are anxious to get on with this today. I think it is pertinent to put the reasons for the need for this legislation on the record, that is, beyond the obvious ones.
We were contemplating the adjournment of this chamber at the end of July, but it was decided that we would move quickly, although I hardly think seven years is too rapid an approach, to deal with this piece of legislation today and to have it looked at by the Senate. It is a matter of some regret that now we are referring this bill to the other place, leaving them only a matter of a few short days in which to contemplate it, review it, and let us have their considered judgment respecting it. It is important to say that. If this bill were not dealt with in the closing days of this session, there is a probability-always we seem to refer to possibilities; I think this is more of a probability-we would have returned to this chamber around Thanksgiving or shortly afterward only to find, because of other pressing matters, an urgency to wind up this session and commence a new one. If that happened, the bill might very well have died, and then it would have been necessary to reintroduce it in all of its stages, thus causing further delay.
It will not be a new session in the fall; it will be the same session.

I do not think this session will last much beyond one or two days after our return. It may; I may be wrong. In any event, it would have called for a total reworking of this particular piece of legislation. That would have been the fifth time around, and it would have been unacceptable.
I hope the Senate is able to consider it and that the matter will be dealt with so that the proper authorities can get on with their two to three-month job of putting together the regulations in the hope of meeting a satisfactory application date for this piece of legislation before December 31, 1980.

Mr. Speaker, it appears that I have the opportunity to give the benediction on the transportation of dangerous goods bill. Although I want to acknowledge the efforts that have gone into the formulation of this legislation-work which long precedes my arrival in this august chamber-I feel that it is somewhat appropriate that I have the opportunity to speak at this stage. My first question in this House was put in October, 1979, to the then minister of the environment, asking when the transportation of dangerous goods bill would be brought forward. It was only a month after that question that the events in Mississauga occurred, and only shortly thereafter that the move to bring in the bill gained momentum. 1 think we need to be reminded of that, Mr. Speaker.
1 am willing to participate in the non-partisan atmosphere which prevails in the House this afternoon, and 1 should like to extend my congratulations to the committee on the work it has done. I was not a member of that committee so I extend my congratulations to it, to my colleagues for the quality of their amendments, to the officials and everyone involved.
With respect to this bill, as with so many other things, we must realize that we are at third reading stage today because incidents like the one at Mississauga happened, and not entirely because of our own foresight.
As I said earlier, the question I asked in October, 1979, concerned not only the transportation of dangerous goods but also the disposal of dangerous goods. I was reminded of that when the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) expressed concern about the transportation of radioactive material. Another concern that many people have about radioactive material is its disposal once the use for which it was being transported has been executed. Of course this concerns not only radioactive material but many other dangerous products as well.
We have to realize two things about the limitations of what we are doing today, Mr. Speaker. It has already been pointed out that the bill is only concerned with the transportation and packaging of dangerous goods and not with the safety of vehicles and transportation systems responsible for carrying those goods. The bill does not address the much longer-term problem of disposal of dangerous goods. This is something that I hope members of the government in particular will note, and that we will not have to wait for an accident like that at Mississauga before we begin to take the problem of disposal of dangerous goods seriously. As a logical extension of the concern of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, I hope we will not wait for a disaster before legislation is brought forward to deal with the disposal of dangerous goods and, in particular, the disposal of radioactive waste. Of course we would not have that problem in the first place if we were to abandon our foolish commitment to nuclear power. It looks as if the government is committed to nuclear power, however, so we must take very seriously the problem of the disposal of radioactive waste.
Perhaps I am something of a party-pooper and am taking the gleam off the mutual admiration society that we seem to have become this afternoon when dealing with passage of this particular bill, Mr. Speaker, but I want to put these points before the House.
Another matter I want to deal with is the concern felt in my home town of Winnipeg. It is unfortunate that the public's attention and heightened awareness of the problem which the transportation of dangerous goods poses has come about as a result of incidents like Mississauga, MacGregor and the methanol spill at the CPR yards at Winnipeg. Unfortunately, this did not lead to a stronger commitment by the federal government to rail relocation in Winnipeg.
One of the ways in which we can reduce the danger to life, to health, to property and the environment, is to take seriously the opportunities to reroute these products in our major residential areas. It seems that in spite of the awareness created through recent events and the debate on this bill, the government has not been inspired to do anything more decisive about railway relocation in Winnipeg-not just for the sake of safety but for the sake of revitalization of the inner city of Winnipeg.
