speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
that Bill C-31, to provide for the imposition of certain economic sanctions against the Islamic Republic of Iran, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
He said: Members are well aware of the circumstances that have led to the introduction of this bill. The seizure by Iranian militants of the American Embassy in Tehran on November 4 last year, and the subsequent detention of its staff, constitute grave violations of international law which call for an unequivocal response from the international community.
The strong protests which Canada and other countries have already made to these violations are not an over-reaction to a mere breach of diplomatic form. On the contrary, the hostage crisis is a fundamental challenge to the centuries-old evolution
Iranian Economic Sanctions Act
of orderly relations among states. Without the assurance that governments can confidently exchange diplomatic missions, and that host governments will accord them immunity and protection from acts of violence such as we have recently seen in Iran and in other countries, interstate co-operation will be in grave danger.
That Iran, over the past year has been trying to evolve new government institutions and has so far lacked centralized authority is, of course, a factor which we must keep in mind in deciding the nature of our response to the hostage crisis. However, the internal situation in Iran cannot in any way be used as an excuse to look the other way when a violation of international law of this magnitude occurs. The international community would do so at its peril.
The threat which this crisis poses for the international community was recognized by the United Nations Security Council, which last December passed without dissent, and with even the support of the Soviet Union, two resolutions urging respect for international law and demanding the release of the hostages. The second resolution called for sanctions against Iran in the event of non-compliance by that country with the terms of the resolution. Its purpose was ultimately frustrated when the Soviet Union vetoed the draft calling for specific sanctions against Iran which the Americans introduced on January 10.
The cynical Soviet veto, however, cannot obscure the fact that the international community, both then and now, condemns the hostage affair. In addition to the overwhelming support given to the Security Council resolutions on Iran, this condemnation from the international community has been reiterated by the International Court of Justice which, first in December and then again in May, ordered Iran to restore the embassy to the U.S.A. and to free the hostages. These unequivocal judgments by the UN and the International Court of Justice fully justify the international community in applying economic sanctions against Iran.
After the sanctions resolution was vetoed on January 13, the American government requested a number of friendly governments, including Canada, to apply the measures foreseen in the resolution, notwithstanding the Soviet veto. This American request was subsequently held in abeyance when it appeared in late January that a more cohesive and pragmatic administration was emerging in Iran, and that the UN might be able to mediate the dispute. Regrettably, that has not proved to be the case. Even now that that Parliament has finally come together, a solution appears to be no nearer.
The decision by the European Economic Community and Japan on April 22, and by Canada on April 23, to impose limited measures against Iran was in response to a renewed call for support from President Carter on April 8. At the time they imposed these limited measures, the EEC, Japan and Canada stated that if there was no decisive progress in the hostage situation by May 17, further measures would be taken against Iran. No decisive progress was achieved, and on May 18, EEC countries, followed by Japan, decided to implement the kind of measures contained in the vetoed Security Council

July 16, 1980
Iranian Economic Sanctions Act resolution. On May 22 I announced that Canada was taking parallel steps by placing controls on the export of goods to Iran and by introducing into the House the legislation to which I am speaking at the moment.
I have already explained that the government has been prompted to take these steps out of its concern to uphold a fundamental rule of international law which is vital to the conduct of international relations. It follows from this preoccupation that we would like to see as many countries as possible support such measures, so as to impress on the Iranians that a prolongation of the hostage situation will inevitably lead to their further isolation in the international community. It was this consideration that led us to co-ordinate our recent actions with the EEC countries, Japan and Australia. It is for the same reason that I hope the House will give immediate approval to this bill, and thus put Canada in a position to implement, in concert with our allies, the range of measures supported by a large majority of the Security Council.
In addition to considerations of legal principle, there are compelling political reasons why Canada and other countries should support economic sanctions against Iran. These measures go at least some way to reassure the Americans that the international community is prepared to show solidarity in confronting an illegal situation that is deeply frustrating and galling to them, and is indeed intolerable for all law-abiding states.
In our view patience is required to allow the Iranian political scene to evolve, and imagination will be needed to find a formula for the safe release of all the hostages. Canada will do what it can to support initiatives that have some chance of securing the hostages' release through negotiation. Meantime, however, we cannot accept that no action be taken. We must demonstrate to the Americans as well as to the Iranians our determination that justice in terms of international law is available to all countries. Economic sanctions, in addition to their value in adding to the pressures on Iran to release the hostages, serve this symbolic purpose.
There is a point I should add about Canadian-Iranian relations in the longer term. 1 have already assured the Iranian foreign minister in a personal message on May 12 that we are not mounting sanctions against Iran because of any hostile attitude toward the Iranian government and people, or out of any desire to intervene in Iran's internal affairs. Canada strongly supports the independence and territorial integrity of Iran. It looks forward to the day when the hostage crisis is resolved and it should once again be possible to resume the full range of friendly contacts between our two countries.
Turning to the nature of the legislation now before the House, the Security Council resolution proposed by the U.S.A. on January 10 required all states to take a number of measures against Iran in the areas of trade, transport, finance and diplomacy. Some of the measures, such as the placing of controls on the export of goods to Iran and restrictions on diplomatic personnel, can be taken by administrative measures in Canada, and this we have already done.
Had the U.S.S.R. not vetoed the resolution, all of the other measures could have been implemented under our United Nations Act. The Soviet veto made this impossible and the government has therefore proposed that Parliament enact new legislation that would enable the imposition of economic sanctions against Iran. The bill follows the draft resolution very closely and is designed to put the government in the same position it would have been in had the Soviet Union not cast their veto.
The government recognizes the exceptional character of this bill and has therefore drafted it in narrow terms intended only for the implementation of the January 10 draft resolution. We have provided an opportunity for parliamentary review and debate of regulations made under the new legislation. The bill also contains provision for its expiry one year after the day it is assented to, unless expressly extended.
In conclusion, let us hope that circumstances will ensure that the need for and hence duration of this legislation will be short-lived. The just announced release of one Iranian hostage appears not to indicate any general change of heart, but once the new Iranian parliament has been able to establish its working procedures it should be able to turn its attention to the hostage question. With their country facing increasingly urgent and difficult problems at home and abroad, more and more Iranians may come to see the hostage crisis as an unnecessary impediment to the solution of these other problems. As soon as the hostages are released, the government will move quickly to repeal the legislation now before us and will resume its efforts to renew relations with Iran, for which we think there is considerable scope.
Although the motion as you have presented it, Mr. Speaker, was to refer this bill to the Standing Committee on International Affairs and National Defence, I believe there may be unanimous disposition on the part of the House to deal with the bill in all stages today after members have finished their speeches on second reading, and I hope that that will be the procedure which is followed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 can inform the House that this party is in agreement that the bill proceed through all stages today, and 1 would like to reassure the minister of that.
In recent days the release of one of the American hostages from Iran has dramatically focused, once again, the world's attention on the detention of American diplomats in Iran, and that makes more relevant the debate we are having on this bill today, which is to provide for the imposition of certain economic sanctions against the Islamic Republic of Iran. We hope and pray, sir, that Mr. Richard Queen's release is no isolated incident, and that his 52 comrades will soon follow his path to freedom.
It is now 255 days since the American embassy in Tehran was overrun by the so-called student militants. It is more than eight long months since the American diplomatic personnel in
July 16, 1980

the U.S. embassy in Tehran were seized as hostages. Throughout this long period, Canadians, of all the peoples in the world, have been front-line observers of the personal anguish and the national anxiety which these events have stirred in our American neighbours. We are reminded daily of their concerns through the medium of television and radio, and through personal contacts with our neighbours to the south.
Canadians are a people who know and cherish our liberties and who understand and respect international order. The flagrant disregard for both of these, that is, of liberties and international order, by the leaders and by the people of Iran, has evoked in Canada a deep and genuine concern for the well-being of the American hostages, and a symphathy for those in the United States administration and in the government who have so patiently worked for the resolution of this crisis.
As Canada's foreign minister at the time of the embassy takeover, 1 was very much aware of the sentiments of Canadians as well as the concern in most nations over the disregard for international law regarding diplomatic immunity. Canadians recognized that the very foundations of international law and civilized diplomacy were being called into question by the situation in Iran.
Canada's involvement in this international crisis was heightened on November 9, five days after the embassy takeover when Ambassador Ken Taylor was authorized by then prime minister Clark to provide refuge to six American diplomatic personnel who were outside the U.S. embassy at the time of the seizure. That decision to offer sanctuary to our American house guests and the vital necessity to keep it a closely guarded secret so as to protect them, made the Canadian government's reaction to events in Tehran more difficult and more complex.
I would like to explain why.
As a government, we were determined to do all we could to lead international opinions, organizations, groups and nations in pressing the Iranian authorities, who were often incapable or unwilling to govern, into releasing the American hostages. We were trying throughout to take a lead in that regard. At the same time we were well aware that initiatives that were too isolated or too high profile, initiatives which would have had the effect of focusing unusual attention on the Canadian embassy, could endanger the American hostages, our house guests, and our own foreign service personnel in Tehran. Yet we were determined to play a vigorous role, both public and private, in seeking a resolution to this situation.
So, on November 27, as a result of a Canadian initiative, a meeting of Commonwealth representatives was held in London. As a result of that meeting a joint communique was issued protesting the actions of the Iranian militants and appealing for the release of the American hostages. Later, on December 4, at the United Nations, Canada welcomed the Security Council resolution calling for the release of the American hostages. On December 13, at the NATO ministerial meetings in Brussels which 1 was attending, the foreign ministers called upon the Iranian authorities to set at liberty the American diplomats.
Iranian Economic Sanctions Act
While these public statements were important, the government recognized that further steps had to be taken, including economic sanctions, and that they should be considered by all concerned nations. This required ongoing consultations if effective sanctions were to be imposed. Because of the secret harbouring of the Americans in our embassy, regular consultation and contact had already begun between Canada and the United States officials as well as between Secretary of State Vance and myself.
In early December I met with senior U.S. officials in Paris to discuss, among other things, economic sanctions against Iran. Indeed, as a result of those meetings, then prime minister Clark privately communicated a set of guidelines to be followed by Canadian banks regarding banking business with Iran. We had also begun other sanctions of an economic nature, some of which are referred to in the legislation before us today.

Because we are neighbours to the United States, we Canadians are aware of the feelings the hostage situation in Iran has aroused among Americans. That is why Canada has acted so promptly to establish various organizations which would help liberate the hostages. Moreover, it was natural that the Clark government readily agreed to lodge the six American diplomats in our embassy in Tehran.
I am proud of the measures taken by the Progressive Conservative government. Our government spared no effort to remedy this shocking incident of hostage-taking in Tehran. My party still strongly supports this approach.
Because Canadians understand, more than any other nation, the enormity of feeling that the hostage situation in Iran has aroused in the American people; because we were so deeply involved in urging various international organizations to seek an earlier resolution to this situation; and because of our overriding concern for the safety of the six Americans and our own personnel in the Canadian embassy in Tehran, it was only natural that, as Canada's foreign minister, I went to New York on December 30 to urge the Security Council to adopt the American resolution calling for the release of the hostages, and if that was not forthcoming, to impose economic sanctions against Iran. This was perhaps not the normal thing to do, given that Canada is not a member of the Security Council at present, but I felt that the circumstances compelled my personal intervention.
In calling for the implementation of economic sanctions, I stated at that Security Council meeting that such action would be "a powerful, positive and peaceful step to help resolve this intolerable situation which threatens the peace, order and good governance of the world".
That American resolution, the text of which is substantially the same as the legislation before us today, was subsequently vetoed by the Soviet Union in the Security Council on January

13. Certainly, sir, if these measures were warranted in January, they are even more deserving of our support six months later, with the American diplomats still being held as hostages.
Securing international support for economic sanctions against Iran has not been easy-indeed their total effectiveness is not assured even after months of consultation. But then nothing about the international effort to free the hostages has been easy; it has involved a very real element of personal risk, delicate diplomacy, and considerable danger, for individuals and countries. That was true when the Canadian government gave refuge to the American diplomats, when we communicated guidelines to the banks, when we spoke out in international forums. But I am very proud of the steps taken by the government of which I was a member. In the face of this outrageous violation of international law in Iran, we did what we could to help resolve the situation. And my party continues to support, and strongly support, that approach and the bill that is before us today.
There is, however, one aspect of this entire episode which has deeply troubled me and many other Canadians, and it concerns the behaviour of the then leader of the opposition, the right hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau). In his role as a Privy Councillor and as leader of the official opposition, he was informed shortly after the decision had been taken to provide sanctuary to the six American diplomats, of this secret and very delicate mission. Presumably he would have understood the danger to these American diplomats if their whereabouts had become known. Presumably he would have recognized the difficult balancing act the government was involved in, in which we were making every effort in various international organizations to seek a resolution of this crisis, including by means of sanctions, but doing it in such a way that would not endanger the lives of our Canadian personnel in Tehran or the safety of those Americans we sought to protect.
And yet day after day, in a partisan fashion, the right hon. member sought to embarrass the government over what he portrayed as the government's lack of action and lack of support for American efforts to release the hostages. As he said to me on November 27, during question period in the House of Commons, "we will soon be condemning this government if it continues to take such standoffish attitudes". Yet he knew better, he was one of the very few to be privy to what was taking place at our embassy in Tehran. I say, sir, that his conduct throughout this period was one of the most cynical displays of opportunism and political gamesmanship this House has ever witnessed.
Hear, hear!

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have read in the past few days that the Iranian acting ambassador to Canada has stated that if Canada's relations with Iran are to improve, we will have to apologize to Iran for helping in the escape of the U.S. diplomats. I am certain, Mr. Speaker, that most Canadians find that piece of gratuitous advice downright insulting.
The rescue operation carried out by Ambassador Taylor and other Canadians, both in Tehran and in Ottawa, is a matter of great national pride. We certainly have no apologies for compassion, for bravery, and for plain good neighbourliness. Our pride, however, is tempered by the fact that there still remain 52 American diplomats in Iran. It is our hope that the sanctions for which this bill provides will be an effective instrument in securing their freedom. To this end, my party supports the bill before us today.

Mr. Speaker, we deeply regret the need for this bill. We have some concerns about it, but we are prepared to give it our support. That includes our willingness, at the conclusion of the second reading debate, that the bill be referred to the Committee of the Whole so that it can be dealt with through all stages before we rise at six o'clock. I said that we have some misgivings or concerns about the bill, but it is a fact, as stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan), that our world is in a bad way if the traditional immunities enjoyed by diplomatic personnel in the countries of this world are violated or diminished, and we have to give very serious consideration to what has developed because of the hostagetaking incident in Iran.
We join with others in expressing our concern for the people of the United States in the long trial they are going through with respect to this matter. We earnestly hope that some time very soon it will be resolved. We are also concerned that there are so many incidents affecting diplomatic personnel in other parts of the world. As I say, we join with others in this House in the belief that this is a matter which deserves very serious consideration.
I said that we have some concerns. I do not intend to spell or spin them out. We note that boycotting by certain other nations is sometimes not carried out very effectively. We know of boycotts which are there on paper but are violated in various ways known to us all. We sometimes wonder whether economic boycotts have any effect in resolving a situation, whether they do anything more than stiffen the spine of those who are boycotted. Yet we are prepared to admit that this situation is so serious that we have to place in the hands of the government the power contained in this bill if the government feels that such power has to be used. I must also say we wish that in circumstances like this our friendly neighbour to the south, the United States, would do a little more consulting before it takes positions and initiates actions which it expects us to follow-this is a view which is understood, I think, by most observers of international relations.
Nevertheless, having said these things, we recognize that the kind of power contained in this bill is something the government should have, and for that reason we are prepared to support the measure.
The main reason this bill is necessary is, of course, because of the hostages being held in Tehran and elsewhere. The other
July 16, 1980

immediate reason was the veto on January 13 by the Soviet Union of the resolution which had been presented to the United Nations Security Council. Had that resolution been passed, this action today would not have been necessary. As the minister has said, this bill simply places the Canadian government in the position in which it would have found itself had that resolution passed. I commend the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the government of which he is a member, on recognizing how serious a matter this is.
This is a temporary piece of legislation. I notice it is to be in effect for one year from the time it is given royal assent, unless it is extended, but that it cannot be extended longer than for a further year. There are also limitations with regard to actions which can be taken under the bill. The government has to lay its proposals before Parliament, and Parliament has the opportunity to approve or negate them as it wishes. These precautions having been taken with respect to a serious operation, we are prepared to support the bill through all its stages this afternoon.

My first question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs at this stage of the bill has to do with a matter which has troubled me-possibly he can allay my concerns. We have read a great deal about these problems in the press. There are many.
